title: Stirling Cycle Numbers
subtitle: Referred to as Stirling Numbers of the First Kind

To inspire this lecture, let us ask a question.

Q: Suppose we have $n$ people with $k$ identical round tables, where each table cannot be left empty. How many ways can you arrange the seating for $n$ people to $k$ tables, where we only count the arrangements in which some person has a different neighbor than previous arrangements? If we only have one table, we know the answer to be $(n-1)!$. 

Let us define this number to be the Stirling Cycle Number, denoted as $[^n_k]$ or $c(n,k)$. This number is also referred to as the **Stirling numbers of the first kind**. For this lecture, we will be using the signless version; the signed version is $(-1)^{n-k}c(n,k)$.
